articles.title: Contrast and Color: Designing for the Way People Actually See
articles.summary: Good contrast is the single most common accessibility gap on the web. Here is where the WCAG numbers come from, why controls need contrast too, and why color must never work alone.

sections.heading: Text contrast: the 4.5:1 rule
sections.body: WCAG asks for 4.5:1 between text and background (3:1 for large text), with 7:1 at the stricter AAA level. The W3C explains that 4.5:1 compensates for the contrast loss of moderately low vision, color deficiencies and aging.

sections.heading: Controls and icons need contrast too
sections.body: WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 for input borders, control states, focus rings and meaningful graphics. A pale gray border on a white page is the classic failure.

sections.heading: Color must never work alone
sections.body: WCAG 1.4.1 says color cannot be the only way to convey meaning. Pair color with underlines, icons or words for links, errors, required fields and status.

sections.heading: Why this is not a niche issue
sections.body: Birch's 2012 review found about 8% of men and 0.4% of women of European descent, and 4% to 6.5% of men of Chinese and Japanese ethnicity, have red-green color deficiency.

articles.body:
Accessible color is not about making a page ugly. It is about making sure the people who visit can actually see what you built. Four sources set the ground rules.

## Text contrast: the 4.5:1 rule and where it comes from

The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2, 2023) require a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 between text and its background, with 3:1 allowed for large text. The W3C's own explanation of Success Criterion 1.4.3 says the 3:1 base figure comes from ISO 9241-3 and an older US standard, and that 4.5:1 compensates for the loss of contrast that comes with moderately low visual acuity (roughly 20/40), color deficiencies or aging. A stricter Level AAA criterion asks for 7:1, which corresponds to roughly 20/80 acuity. The rule applies to placeholder text and to text that appears on hover or focus, not only to headings and paragraphs, and real text placed over a photo is still measured against what sits behind it, so hero headlines need a solid or gradient panel behind them rather than hope.

To make this concrete: mid-gray #767676 on white just clears 4.5:1 (about 4.54:1), while #595959 on white reaches 7:1.

## Controls and icons need contrast too

WCAG 1.4.11 (added in WCAG 2.1) extends contrast to things that are not text. Visual information needed to identify a control or its state, such as an input border, a checkbox state or a focus ring, needs at least 3:1 against adjacent colors, and so do the parts of a graphic needed to understand it. The classic failure is a pale gray input border on a white page: the field is there, but a person with low vision may not find it. Inactive controls are exempt.

## Color must never work alone

WCAG 1.4.1 (Level A, the most basic tier) says color must not be the only way to convey information, indicate an action, prompt a response or distinguish an element. Typical failures include links in body text that differ only in color, errors shown only by a red outline, or required fields marked only by color. The W3C's technique for links is to give them at least 3:1 contrast with the surrounding text plus an extra cue on hover and focus, and underlining is the simplest way to avoid the problem altogether.

## Why this is not a niche issue

Jennifer Birch's 2012 review in the Journal of the Optical Society of America A pulled together large population surveys of inherited red-green color deficiency. Among people of European descent, about 8% of men and 0.4% of women are affected, and among men of Chinese and Japanese ethnicity the figure is between 4% and 6.5%. Those numbers vary by population, and color deficiency is only one reason people miss color cues, since low vision, aging screens and bright sunlight all matter too.

## Putting it together

Pick your palette by contrast first and hue second. Check every text and background pair, including text on images, placeholders and hover states. Give inputs and icons a visible 3:1 edge. And for anything that carries meaning, such as status, errors or plan tiers, pair the color with a word, an icon or a pattern.

articles.title: Focus, Motion and Moving Parts: Keeping Landing Pages Usable
articles.summary: Sticky headers, carousels, background video and parallax are popular landing page features and common barriers. Three W3C criteria explain how to keep them usable.

sections.heading: Sticky headers can hide the keyboard focus
sections.body: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 says a control receiving keyboard focus must not be entirely hidden by author-created content. Test by tabbing through the page and offset scroll positions so focused items land below fixed headers.

sections.heading: Anything that moves by itself needs an off switch
sections.body: WCAG 2.2.2 requires a way to pause, stop or hide automatic motion that lasts more than five seconds. That covers auto-rotating carousels and background videos.

sections.heading: Scroll effects can make people ill
sections.body: WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) targets interaction-triggered motion such as parallax, which can trigger vestibular disorders. Honor the reduce-motion setting or offer a control.

articles.body:
Modern landing pages love sticky headers, sliding carousels, looping videos and parallax scrolling. Each can be a barrier for someone. Three W3C criteria describe how.

## Sticky headers can hide the keyboard focus

People who use a keyboard move through a page with the Tab key, and a visible focus indicator shows where they are. WCAG 2.2 added Success Criterion 2.4.11, Focus Not Obscured (Minimum, Level AA): when a control receives keyboard focus it must not be entirely hidden by author-created content. Sticky headers, cookie banners and chat widgets are the usual culprits. If a fixed header covers the field you just tabbed into, you cannot see what you are typing into. Partial overlap is allowed at AA; the stricter AAA version (2.4.12) does not allow any overlap. In practice this means testing by tabbing forwards and backwards through the whole page, and offsetting scroll positions (for example with CSS scroll-padding) so focused items land below the header. Content the user opens themselves, such as a dialog they can dismiss with Esc, is treated more leniently.

## Anything that moves by itself needs an off switch

WCAG 2.2.2, Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A), applies to moving, blinking or scrolling content that starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds and appears alongside other content. Users must be able to pause, stop or hide it. Auto-updating content must also be controllable, and there is no five-second exception for it. The W3C explains why: moving content is a barrier for people who read slowly or have trouble tracking motion, it can cause problems for screen readers, and it can be a severe distraction for some people, including those with attention deficits. Auto-rotating hero carousels and background videos are the everyday examples. The simplest solutions are a static hero, or a visible, keyboard-operable pause button.

## Scroll effects can make people ill

WCAG 2.3.3, Animation from Interactions (Level AAA), is about motion triggered by the user's own actions, such as parallax scrolling where backgrounds move at a different speed from foregrounds. The W3C notes that such effects can trigger vestibular disorders, with dizziness, nausea and headaches, and that reactions can be severe. Non-essential animation should be avoidable: skip the effect, offer a control to turn it off, or honor the operating system's reduce-motion setting through the CSS prefers-reduced-motion media query. This criterion is Level AAA, which is above the AA level that many accessibility laws and policies refer to, but honoring reduced motion is cheap and increasingly expected.

## A practical checklist

- Tab through the page with a sticky header on, and confirm every focused item stays visible.
- Give any auto-playing motion longer than five seconds a pause control, or remove the autoplay.
- Wrap parallax and large transforms in a reduced-motion check, and fall back to a simple fade or no animation.

None of these ideas require giving up polish. They ask for control: the visitor decides what moves.

Understanding SC 2.3.3: Animation from Interactions, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1

articles.title: Structure, Labels and Forms That Work With Assistive Technology
articles.summary: Screen readers, voice control and keyboards depend on the code behind the design. The biggest audit of the web shows the same handful of gaps year after year, and they are mostly design decisions.

sections.heading: What the biggest audit finds
sections.body: WebAIM's 2026 analysis of one million home pages found six error types account for 96% of detected failures: low contrast, missing alt text, missing form labels, empty links, empty buttons and missing page language.

sections.heading: Decide what every image is for
sections.body: The W3C sorts images into informative, decorative, functional and complex, each with a different text alternative. Icon-only links and buttons need alt text describing the action.

sections.heading: Headings are how screen reader users navigate
sections.body: In WebAIM's 2024 survey, 71.6% of screen reader users first navigate long pages by headings. Use real heading elements in a logical order with descriptive text.

sections.heading: Placeholders are not labels
sections.body: NN/g's testing shows placeholder-as-label strains memory, hides errors and is often low contrast or unread. Use visible labels outside the field.

articles.body:
Screen readers, voice control and keyboards all depend on the code behind the design. Four sources show where landing pages most often fall short and what to do about it.

## What the biggest audit finds

WebAIM, the accessibility group at Utah State University, analyzes the home pages of the top million websites every year. Its 2026 report found detectable WCAG failures on 95.9% of pages, and six error types made up 96% of everything it detected: low-contrast text (83.9% of pages), missing alternative text on images (53.1%), missing form labels (51%), empty links (46.3%), empty buttons (30.6%) and a missing page language (13.5%). These are the same six categories as in each of the previous seven years. WebAIM also found that pages using ARIA averaged 59.1 detected errors against 42 for pages without, and that popular carousel libraries were associated with more errors than average, though it cautions that these pages are also more complex, so the link is correlational.

Nothing in that list requires a redesign. It requires a few deliberate decisions in the design system.

## Decide what every image is for

The W3C's images tutorial (which supports WCAG 1.1.1) sorts images into four kinds. Informative images need a short description of the essential information. Decorative images get an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip them. Functional images, such as an icon inside a button or link, need alt text that describes the action, for example 'View pricing', rather than the picture. Complex images such as charts need a short description plus the underlying information nearby. In WebAIM's data, 16.2% of all images lacked alt text, and 45% of those were linked images, which leaves links without a meaningful name.

## Headings are how screen reader users navigate

In WebAIM's Screen Reader User Survey #10 (1,539 respondents, collected in December 2023 and January 2024), 71.6% said that on a long page they first navigate through the headings, and 88.8% found heading levels very or somewhat useful. Only 3.7% started with landmarks. The sample was not controlled, so it may not represent all screen reader users, but the direction is clear: use real heading elements in a logical order, with descriptive text, so each section of the landing page can be found on its own. WebAIM's audit also shows how often this goes wrong: skipped heading levels appeared on 41.8% of pages.

## Placeholders are not labels

Katie Sherwin's Nielsen Norman Group article summarizes user testing showing that placeholder text used in place of a label strains memory, prevents people from checking their entries, is skipped as if it were pre-filled, and is often low contrast or not read aloud by screen readers. NN/g's best option is a visible label, with any hint, outside the field. Floating labels are an acceptable compromise where space is tight, but they do not fix every problem.

## Takeaway

Give every input a visible label, every icon-only control a name, every image a purpose, and every section a real heading. Those four habits cover a large share of the failures that automated audits find.

articles.title: Text People Can Read: Spacing, Fonts, Size and Cognitive Load
articles.summary: Readable text is spacing, letterforms, size and how much you ask people to hold in their heads. Four sources give concrete guidance, with honest limits.

sections.heading: Let people change the spacing
sections.body: WCAG 1.4.12 requires nothing to break when readers override line height, paragraph, letter and word spacing. Buttons with fixed heights and non-wrapping labels are the usual failures.

articles.body:
Readable text is not one setting. It is spacing, letterforms, size and how much you ask people to hold in their heads. Four sources give concrete guidance.

## Let people change the spacing

WCAG 1.4.12 (Level AA) does not tell you to set your text a particular way. It says nothing should break when a reader overrides the spacing: line height up to 1.5 times the font size, paragraph spacing to 2 times, letter spacing to 0.12 times and word spacing to 0.16 times. People with low vision or dyslexia often use extensions or style sheets to do exactly this. The usual failures are buttons with fixed heights that clip their labels, tab labels that overflow and cards whose text is hidden. The fix is to let containers grow: use minimum heights, allow wrapping and test with a text-spacing bookmarklet.

## Fonts: sans serif helped in one dyslexia study

Luz Rello and Ricardo Baeza-Yates (2013, ACM ASSETS) used eye tracking with 48 people with dyslexia reading 12 fonts. Sans serif, monospaced and roman styles improved reading performance compared with serif, proportional and italic ones. Helvetica, Courier, Arial, Verdana and Computer Modern Unicode came out best, and the specially designed OpenDyslexic font gave no advantage in this study. The caveat: the study did not control how far apart each font sets its letters, so some of the effect may come from spacing. The practical reading is modest and useful: a plain sans serif body font without italics is a safe default, and you do not need a specialty font.

## Size: bigger than most designers set it

Rello, Pielot and Marcos (2016, ACM CHI) ran an eye-tracking study with 104 participants reading Wikipedia text at six sizes from 10 to 26 points. Readability and comprehension improved up to 18 points, and comprehension questions were answered best at 18 and 26 points. Extreme line spacings (0.8 and 1.8 times default) marginally hurt readability, while ordinary variations made little difference. Their advice for text-heavy pages is 18-point text or larger with default line spacing. The study covered desktop reading of long articles by people aged 14 to 54, so treat it as evidence for continuous reading text, not for small interface labels.

## Cognitive load: familiar beats clever

The W3C's cognitive accessibility note, Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (2021), is supplemental guidance rather than a requirement of WCAG. Its patterns are practical: state the purpose of each page clearly, use familiar layouts and standard-looking links and buttons, put the most important tasks near the top, use short chunks of content with white space, avoid content that moves unexpectedly, and use plain, literal wording. It also asks that users can control content that moves or changes. The note says these patterns help many people, including those under stress or new to the web, and are essential for some.

## Putting it together

Set body text generously, use a neutral sans serif, and make the layout tolerant of user overrides. Then keep the page itself calm and predictable.
